prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought the measurement of time and frequency to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B031 as a single prize part, and I am somewhat more confident than before because the objections have narrowed to two questions: distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and priority at the margin. On distinctness, the chair asks for the decisive physical step. For me it is this. A single trapped ion (Wineland) gives superb control, but the signal comes from one quantum system, so stability is limited by atom number. The comb (Hall, Hansch) counts optical cycles and is needed by every optical clock, but it does not itself supply the reference. The lattice clock is the step where many neutral atoms are held in a standing wave at the magic wavelength, so that the two clock levels shift equally and the trap does not perturb the transition, with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed in the Lamb-Dicke regime. That combines the ion's freedom from motional effects with the atom number of a neutral-atom ensemble. It is what made 1e-18-level stability reachable in practical averaging times, and it is what opened density-dependent and many-body effects, millimetre-scale redshift measurements and searches for varying constants and dark matter. A citation that names magic-wavelength trapping states this step and keeps the prize from reading as a second comb prize. On maturity, several independent laboratories reproduce and compare clocks at the 1e-18 level, which is the reproducibility I weigh most. The redefinition of the second is a roadmap item, not a condition for recognising a physics result that has already been realised and reproduced, so I would not wait for it. Attribution is the most defensible on the shortlist: Katori for the proposal and first demonstration, Ye for taking accuracy, stability and the many-body regime to the frontier.
statement.case_against: The reservations remain real. A sceptic can still read the lattice clock as an exceptional refinement of optical frequency standards that the committee has already honoured twice in two decades, and whether an instrument counts as a discovery is a judgment that I cannot settle with evidence. The priority record is incomplete in my own recollection. Takamoto worked in Katori's group, so his early strontium work seems to me to fall within Katori's credit, but the contributions of Lemonde (the mercury lattice scheme and SYRTE work), Ludlow, Oates and the NIST and JILA teams on systematics are separate, and I cannot verify from the files that two names capture the decisive credit. Two names leave out good people, and that is a cost. The headline applications (redefinition of the second, geodesy, dark-matter searches) are still prospective. Finally, B031 would add to a run of atomic and optical prizes (2005, 2012, 2023), and the committee should ask whether balance across fields should count for anything.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B031 eighth in the opening, but in round 1 he names it as his first alternative to B024, calls it mature, reproduced at the 1e-18 level in many laboratories with an uncontested two-person attribution, and says it is the safer choice if maturity and attribution weigh more than conceptual novelty.
responses.response: Your own file moves most of the way toward my position. You trust results where the mechanism is understood and not merely observed, and the lattice clock fits that: the magic-wavelength condition is a derivable statement about the differential polarizability of the two clock levels, and the systematic budget is understood term by term and checked clock against clock. The novelty objection is the one you carried from the opening. The step that separates the lattice clock from combs and ion clocks is the simultaneous interrogation of many neutral atoms without a trap-induced shift, which is a different mechanism from either. I would ask whether the remaining gap between us is novelty as such, or the weight you give to conceptual newness over maturity, since on maturity and attribution your file already grants the point.

responses.point: Eriksson argues that twisted bilayer graphene follows a clean prediction-then-discovery pattern, that eight years of independent replication across groups is a stronger record than some earlier prizes had, and that B031 is the safer choice if maturity and attribution carry the room.
responses.response: I accept the replication argument: many groups have reproduced the correlated insulating and superconducting phases and the field has spread to other moire systems, which is not a small thing. My difficulty is about what exactly is being credited. A citation built on flat bands and correlated states is something I can support scientifically, but the superconducting phase in the same samples is still unexplained, and twist-angle disorder and sample-to-sample variation limit quantitative comparison with the continuum model. The first experimental author of the 2018 papers is also outside the three names, as you and Mehlig both acknowledge. From my own field I know how long a striking observation takes to become a controlled platform. I do not think B024 is wrong, only earlier, and I did not change my configuration because of it. I would gladly look at it again in a later year.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B005, the Higgs discovery, as the most fundamental and best-confirmed result, proposes Gianotti, Jenni and Della Negra anchored in founding leadership and the 2012 spokesperson role, and concedes that attribution is the main difficulty and that B031 has the cleaner credit line.
responses.response: I agree with you on the science, and I think it is the largest unrecognised experimental result of the era. I keep it as an alternative and not as my preferred part because of the point you partly state yourself. The trio mixes founder and spokesperson roles, so the rule that selects Gianotti is not the rule that selects Virdee, and the members who propose trios from the same four names do not agree (your trio and Mehlig's include Gianotti, while Pearce, Johansson and I proposed Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee in our openings). A citation has to be defensible by a stated rule. Without a principle that I can state and that is as strong as the one for Katori and Ye, I do not want to rank an attribution I cannot defend above one I can. If you can state a rule, for example who decided the detector concepts and who led at the time of the discovery, I will listen, but it would have to survive a check of the roles that none of us has verified.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B031 but is less confident than I am that the NIST strontium and Lemonde contributions can be set aside, asks for a check of the priority record before the final ballot, and wants the citation worded around the invention and realisation of the lattice clock and not around the comb.
responses.response: I accept the correction and I agree with the wording, which I have adopted by naming magic-wavelength trapping. On priority I was too quick in round 1. As I recall it, Katori's magic-wavelength proposal dates to roughly 2001 to 2003, his group made the first strontium lattice spectroscopy in the following years, and NIST and JILA then took systematic uncertainty and stability to the frontier, with Lemonde and colleagues contributing the mercury scheme and SYRTE comparisons. That ordering makes Katori the originator and Ye the one who delivered the performance that made the idea convincing, with the others as important parallel and confirming work. But this is recalled and not checked, and I would not claim certainty. If the committee's check of the record shows that Lemonde or another colleague had a decisive and separable step, I would reopen the credit, but under a three-name limit the more defensible reading remains Katori and Ye.

responses.point: Olsson moved from B009 to B031 after the openings, still sees B009 as the better answer if the committee wants an instrument invention that transformed a field, but now weighs the Krivanek attribution problem and thin support too heavily, and notes that a B031 plus B009 pair would need five names.
responses.response: I agree that two parts cannot be offered within the three-person limit without dropping a laureate, which is why I stay with a single part. I also take the Krivanek point seriously: the parallel development of the STEM corrector alongside the TEM correctors means the three supplied names may not capture the decisive credit, and that is why I have moved B009 out of my alternatives. I keep my view that an instrument that opens a new way of observing nature deserves the committee's attention, but I now think that case is better made by B031, where the instrument carries a physical idea (magic-wavelength trapping), than by B009 as currently credited. If B009 returns in a later year with corrected credit, I would support looking at it again.

responses.point: Pearce moved from B005 to B031 after the openings, keeps B005 as his first alternative, and in the chair summary asks whether any member wants a second part and how much recent atomic and optical prizes should weigh against candidates from the same area.
responses.response: I welcome the move, and I share your instrument builder's instinct that a new measurement capability whose systematics are understood and have been checked against rival devices is a firm foundation. On the chair's timing question, I think the 2005, 2012 and 2023 prizes are a legitimate check on balance but should not count against B031 on the science: the physics is distinct, and holding back a mature result because neighbouring work was recognised earlier would penalise it for sitting in an active field. On a second part, I cannot find one that fits within three names and strengthens the citation, so I would keep the prize to one achievement. I also agree with you that the Higgs should not be dropped simply because three-person attribution is awkward, which is why it stays in my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts many-atom magic-wavelength trapping as a distinct achievement and not a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 work; I have argued for it but it remains a judgment.
The priority record among Katori, Takamoto, Ye, Ludlow, Oates and Lemonde, which I am recalling from memory and which nobody in the room has checked against the literature.
Whether a prize limited to Katori and Ye would be read as unfair to other early lattice-clock contributors, and how much that should matter.
Whether the expected redefinition of the second would make this prize look timely or late, and whether to wait for it.
Whether the Higgs discovery, which I consider scientifically first rate, can be defended with three names by a stated rule; I could not state one.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict for B031: I have no collaboration with Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock groups. I repeat my earlier disclosure for transparency: my PhD stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder is a distant mentor-network tie to the JILA tradition behind Ye's group, and I do not regard it as requiring recusal. For B016 (circuit QED), my WACQT role overlaps institutionally with Chalmers, where Goran Johansson has flagged his own connection, so I would defer on B016 if it were taken up. I have no ties to the credited names of B005, B009, B024 or B028.
